### Reviewer 2

Referee Report
Title: Correcting Black Hole Masses Biased by Size Inertia in Broad Line Regions
Recommendation: Reject
Summary
This manuscript presents a study based on a two-epoch spectroscopic analysis of a sample of low-redshift AGNs, with the
goal of improving single-epoch black hole mass estimates. The approach centers on using [O III] luminosity as a proxy for
the ionizing luminosity, under the assumption that it provides a more stable indicator of the BLR radius over time.
The topic is timely and relevant, as improving the reliability of mass estimators is crucial for understanding AGN
demographics and evolution. However, there are serious concerns about both the methodology and the physical
interpretation adopted by the authors. The manuscript does not, in its current form, provide sufficient justification for its core
assumptions and does not meet the standard for publication in Nature Communications.
Major Comments
Use of FWHM and Line Width Assumptions
The most fundamental issue is the use of FWHM as a velocity width indicator in the virial mass formula, and the assumption
that black hole mass scales with the square of FWHM. This is particularly problematic in the context of a study on variability,
where FWHM responds differently than the line dispersion (sigma_line) to continuum flux changes. Since line width enters
t enters
the mass estimate as a power-law (typically squared), a poorly behaved velocity measure like FWHM introduces significant
uncertainty. The authors do not explore how FWHM compares to sigma_line under varying luminosity, nor do they justify
their choice. Simply assuming FWHM is an appropriate measure in this context is not acceptable.
Use of [O III] as a Proxy for Ionizing Flux
The use of [O III] flux as a proxy for the ionizing flux also raises concerns. While the authors mention potential advantages,
they do not consider significant drawbacks. First, [O III] luminosity reflects the time-averaged state of the continuum over
years to decades, due to both light-travel and recombination timescales. In contrast, H-beta responds on reverberation
timescales, which are much shorter and more relevant for BLR dynamics. Second, [O III] is produced by much higher energy
photons than those driving Balmer line emission. Empirically, the study by Greene et al. (2010) shows that the BLR radius
scales more tightly with H-beta luminosity than with [O III], and with less scatter. The authors have not provided any evidence
that [O III] is a better or even comparable proxy to H-beta.
Conceptual Clarifications
In the introduction, the manuscript refers to virial breathing as an “assumption,” when it is actually a predicted consequence
of the standard reverberation mapping interpretation under virial dynamics.
The statement that the variable part of the line may have a different velocity distribution than the mean line is technically
correct, but empirical studies show that line widths in mean and variable spectra are highly correlated.
--------------
Presentation of NGC 5548 and Figures
The analysis of NGC 5548 is reduced to a single data point in Figure 1, despite the long history of monitoring and variability.
It would be more informative to show a range or distribution.
Figure 2 shows changes in H-beta to [O III] ratios over a 20-year interval. The figure is difficult to interpret quantitatively as
the x-axis is not clearly defined. Moreover, a change of 0.26 dex in flux over two decades is not surprising and likely
common among AGNs.
On [O III] Variability Timescales
The claim that [O III] luminosity remains constant over human timescales is incorrect. Long-term monitoring has shown that
[O III] can vary. The more accurate assumption in prior work is that [O III] remains approximately constant over BLR
reverberation timescales, not over decades.
Terminology and References
Terminology should follow standard spectroscopic conventions. For example, the line should be referred to as [O III]
lambda5007, not lambda 5007 [O III].
Table 2 relies on outdated virial product estimates. More recent results are available in Dalla Bonta et al. (2020) for most
objects, as well as in Bentz et al. (2023, ApJ, 944, 29) for IC 4329A, Du et al. (2015, ApJ, 806, 22) for Mrk 1044, and Bentz et
al. (2021, ApJ, 906, 50) for NGC 3783.
Conclusion
The manuscript does not provide a convincing justification for its methodological choices, particularly the use of FWHM and
[O III] luminosity as primary inputs to the mass scaling relation. The results do not offer clear new insight into the physics of
AGN mass estimation and do not meet the threshold of novelty or rigor expected for this journal.

### Reviewer 3

We have read “Correcting Black Hole Masses Biased by Size Inertia in Broad Line Regions” by Amrutha et al. This
manuscript reports analysis of spectral data of active galactic nuclei (AGN) that had previously been observed roughly two
decades earlier. The authors study the joint variability in the width of the H-beta line and the bolometric luminosity (as
measured by 5100 Angstrom continuum measurement and others). Based on their analysis the authors find that the joint
variability is not well described by the prevailing model (the “breathing” broad line region [BLR] model). This, in particular,
has implications for mass estimations of the AGN black holes. The authors then advocate for use of the [O III] luminosity
instead of other luminosity indicators (5100 continuum, H-beta, or combinations with Fe line complex luminosities).
We feel that the potential result is interesting, but there are a number of concerns that prevent us from being able to
determine whether the conclusions are sound. The authors will need to address our major concerns before we can
recommend publication.
*** MAJOR CONCERNS ***
A key concern is the experimental setup. The authors are comparing 6dFGS spectra taken on Schmidt with WiFeS spectra
taken on the ANU 2.3-m telescope. Small systematic differences in the different data sets (even though they were reduced
and fitted with the same procedure) could lead to the appearance of a problem in the model when it is in the data. Is it
possible to directly compare the instrumental setups for consistency? While the authors have the NGC 5548 data that should
be self-consistent, the trend within NGC 5548 is far less convincing.
Related to the above, measurement uncertainties are not addressed in the manuscript at all. It is essential to understand
how measurement uncertainties are incorporated in the analysis. This is especially important when some of the effects that
are being reported are slight (e.g., the difference between 5100 and [O III] scatter in mass measurements is only 0.035 dex).
The correlations of uncertainties between continuum and line widths is a particularly problematic aspect that needs to be
addressed. The fact that the Baldwin effect was not mentioned nor any attempt to mitigate it is particularly worrisome. It is not
possible to publish this work without a thorough examination of how this effect plays a role in the analysis.
A key test of whether what the authors see is real would be to simulate observations with realistic correlated uncertainties
that vary according to the R–L relation with an intrinsic scatter. How often does the simulated Delta FWHM vs Delta L
correlation show the same trend (or more extreme) than the data do?
Measurement uncertainties also need to be taken into account when measuring 16–18 percentiles in Fig 4 and rms in Fig 5.

The latter is better for estimating black hole masses more precisely; the former is better for understanding the physics.

## Paper

## Abstract

Active galactic nuclei (AGN) with broad emission line regions (BLRs) contain rapidly growing supermassive black holes. Their masses are typically derived from BLR gas motions inferred from spectra and BLR sizes estimated from the AGN luminosity. The breathing BLR model predicts that the spectral line width should change as luminosity varies, keeping mass estimates constant. Here, we present observations of an AGN sample at redshift < 0.1 with two epochs separated by 20 years. On average, we find that luminosity and mass estimates vary by a factor of 2, showing a long-term mean-reversion pattern, while the line widths remain constant. A constant line width suggests that full BLRs do not change size during continuum or line flux variability, naturally explaining why scaling relations depend on instantaneously measured Eddington ratios. As a result, we find that single-epoch masses with the best repeatability after 20 years are obtained when sizes are estimated from the narrow [OIII] λ5007 Å emission line luminosity.

---

## Introduction

The origin of supermassive black holes (SMBHs) and the history of their growth in the Universe is one of the most highly debated questions in cosmology1,2. Robust measurements of black hole masses are crucial to this topic and almost always rely on diagnosing the motion of material in orbit around the SMBH. In practice, nearly all known SMBHs are so distant that mass measurements rely on estimates of the orbital sizes of the broad emission line region (BLR) located light-days from the SMBH, and on the velocities of the gas emitting in the BLR, while assuming approximately Keplerian motion3–5. The gas motions are probed through the projected line-of-sight velocity that is reflected in the width of the broad emission lines in active galactic nuclei (AGN) spectra and likely depends on viewing angle6.

The traditional method to estimate the size of the BLR, R_BLR, is reverberation mapping (RM), which measures a time delay between a variable continuum band (used as a proxy for the ionising continuum) and its response in the flux of a spectral emission line emitted from the BLR7,8. The RM method relies on long-term monitoring, which is resource-intensive or even impractical in the large BLRs of rapidly growing SMBHs observed at high redshift. Hence, a much simpler method, known as the virial single-epoch (SE) method9–15, has become the standard and has been applied to several hundred thousand objects accounting for over 99% of all measured SMBHs16–18. While observationally efficient, requiring only a single spectrum, it is less precise, since R_BLR is inferred from AGN luminosity such as the continuum at 5100Å, L_5100, or broad Hβ λ4861Å emission, L_Hβ, using empirical relations calibrated against low-redshift RM measurements. In either method, the SMBH mass is

M_BH = f \frac{v^2 R_BLR}{G}, (1)

where v is the projected line-of-sight velocity and R_BLR is the radius of the BLR, G is the gravitational constant, and f is a dimensionless virial factor that accounts for the uncertain geometry and orientation of the BLR, as well as the relation between the measured RM lags and line widths19. Many studies have sought to refine size-luminosity (R_BLR − L) relations and improve mass estimates by using the luminosity of broad emission lines or the accretion disc continuum as proxies for the ionising radiation20–24. Generally, a large scatter is observed in empirical R_BLR − L relations25, prompting searches for secondary parameters that drive the offsets and methods to calibrate their influence on mass estimates26,27. Here, we present evidence for an alternative approach to SE mass estimation, motivated by global population observations, that does not require invoking a second parameter.

In addition to the global R_BLR − L relation defined by RM samples, individual AGN often show larger lags during epochs of higher continuum luminosity28,29. This behaviour, called virial breathing, arises when increased luminosity shifts the responsivity-weighted BLR radius outward, producing longer lags but with a slope shallower than that of the ensemble R_BLR − L relation25,30. If the BLR response centroid does not vary linearly with the ionising luminosity, deviations from the R_BLR − L relation and corresponding variations in mass estimates will occur. The best-studied case, NGC 5548, has been monitored with nearly 1600 spectra over 43 years31. Evidence for breathing has been reported4,32, but this AGN has also exhibited BLR holidays, during which emission lines and continuum flux variations were decorrelated33,34. One study claims a time delay of 3.5 years in the response of R_BLR and the FWHM of the broad emission lines to changes in luminosity35. Since luminosity varies stochastically on much shorter timescales, the AGN in NGC 5548 is rarely in equilibrium, instead fluctuating around its long-term mean R_BLR − L relation. Observations by the SDSS RM project30 over much shorter periods than for NGC 5548 have produced a broad range of behaviour, but the median width-luminosity slope is shallower than the slope predicted by virial breathing.

It is important to recognise that RM and SE methods probed different parts of the BLR. A single spectrum captures all photons from the BLR, reflecting the integrated velocity distribution, whereas RM isolates only the variable component of an emission line, via an RMS profile from multiple epochs8. This variable component is the one observed to breathe across campaigns. RMS line widths are typically broader than the mean FWHM, though strongly correlated, consistent with the total line emission being more Lorentzian in shape36; this implies that the inner BLR responds more strongly than the outer regions. Therefore, the RM-based lag traces a response-weighted R_BLR, distinct from the emission-weighted R_BLR inferred from SE spectra, and breathing behaviour of the latter has not been conclusively established. Moreover, RM-based R_BLR values depend on the characteristic variability timescale of the continuum, introducing additional scatter into the R_BLR − L relations37,38. Differences in these observational techniques are often cited as the reason for the scatter in SE mass estimates.

In this study, we investigate the repeatability of SE mass measurements in a volume-complete AGN sample. From archival spectra of over 125,000 nearby galaxies in the hemispheric 6-degree Field Galaxy Survey (6dFGS39), a set of 574 broad line AGN complete at K < 12.65 mag was identified40. Of these, 323 AGN at z < 0.1 were observed after a mean time separation of 18.5 years (17.5 years rest frame) with the ANU 2.3 m telescope at Siding Spring Observatory. See Methods for our sample selection criteria, primarily involving the detection of broad Hβ emission in both epochs of observations. This sample has a median bolometric AGN luminosity log(L_bol = erg s^-1) of 44.2, a median SMBH mass log(M_BH = M_sun) of 7.5, and a median Eddington ratio of about 0.05 (Fig. 1; Table 1). The 20-year time separation allows us to see AGN in the least correlated state currently possible, while keeping their true SMBH masses effectively constant. This time separation is similar (for f = 1) or longer than the orbital period (for f > 1) for the median BLR radius and orbital velocity of the 6dFGS AGN sample (see Table 1). In addition, we analyse high-cadence spectroscopic data of NGC 5548, generating 2389 pairs of spectra separated by 17–20 years to mimic the two-epoch design. While these pairs capture the behaviour of a single AGN in detail, the 6dFGS sample represents the broader AGN population.

---

## Results

A 20-year comparison of black hole mass diagnostics
Comparing the pairs of spectra of AGN in the 6dFGS sample separated by about 20 years, we find strong changes in the strength of the continuum and broad emission lines (see example spectra in Fig. 1). In Fig. 2, we show the change in broad Hβ flux for the whole sample, ordered by the relative strength of broad to narrow lines in the 6dFGS epoch as expressed in the ratio Hβ/[OIII]. The average AGN is seen to change by nearly a factor of 2 (Δlog L_Hβ = 0.26 dex) over the 20 years, even after excluding more than 60 changing-look AGN in which the broad Hβ line is absent in one of the epochs41. While it is not unexpected for a single AGN to show variability of this amplitude, it is perhaps surprising that the global AGN population shows on average this level of variability in just 20 years. We note the pattern of mean reversion, whereby previously weak AGN have preferentially strengthened and vice versa, which is expected in a bounded distribution. Otherwise, if all members of a population were evolving along a symmetric random walk, the population would rapidly disperse.

In addition to the Hβ/[OIII] ratio changes, we compare changes in the FWHM of the broad Hβ line, FWHM(Hβ), as a function of changes in the broad-line luminosity, L_Hβ, and the continuum luminosity, L_5100.

We find that the majority of AGN undergo strong luminosity variations without the associated variation in FWHM(Hβ) that would be the signature of virial breathing (see Fig. 3). As the luminosity variability fails to drive the expected change in R_BLR inferred from an instantaneous spectrum, a behaviour we call size inertia of the BLR, AGN in general appear to deviate from the mean R_BLR − L relation continuously and stochastically. This expected change in R_BLR assumes that the BLR gas emitting Hβ is virialised at all radii, that variations in the ionising flux merely shift the effective emitting radius, and that the single-epoch FWHM reliably traces R_BLR.

The change in FWHM(Hβ) has a standard deviation of 0.12 dex in the 6dFGS sample, with a reduced χ2 of 6.6 for a model of ΔFWHM(Hβ) = 0, indicating real variation in FWHM(Hβ). Changes in luminosity and line widths that do not correlate in the direction expected in the breathing model due to the size inertia of the BLR lead to changes in the mass estimate. The 20-year repeatability of the Hβ-derived SE mass has a 68% confidence interval of 0.47 dex width and a 95% confidence interval of 1.29 dex, suggesting a 1σ error of 0.33 dex for any individual snapshot measurement (0.47 = \sqrt{2} * 0.33 dex). This uncertainty reflects only the statistical error from long-term repeatability and does not account for calibration uncertainties of the R_BLR − L relation itself. In NGC 5548 (Fig. 3b, d), we see the same behaviour in the dominant core of the distribution, although an outer contour of rarer behaviour hints at episodes of virial breathing. Figure 4 shows the time evolution of spectral measurements and mass estimates: from 1986 to 2010, the virial SE black hole mass estimate appears to rise by over 0.5 dex.

In Fig. 5, we compare the single-epoch (SE) mass estimates in the 6dFGS sample, separated by two decades, using different proxies for R_BLR. The intrinsic scatter in the differences is 0.47 dex for L_Hβ-based and 0.45 dex for L_5100-based SE masses (16th-84th percentile). Beyond the scatter in L_Hβ and L_5100-derived SE mass estimates, the difference across the two epochs correlate with the ratio between broad and narrow line strength (Fig. 5b); an often used ratio to denote Seyfert subtypes42 (from 1.0 to 1.8) is Hβ/[OIII].

If the R_BLR − L relation does exist across a sample, what is the best proxy for BLR size that pairs with the observed linewidth to yield the most accurate black hole mass? Both the line luminosity, L_Hβ, and the host galaxy-subtracted AGN continuum luminosity, L_5100, vary rapidly. In contrast, the narrow-line luminosity L_[OIII] is a diagnostic of AGN power where short-term variability is suppressed by blending signals with a broad range of time delays, given that the [OIII] emission originates in regions spanning hundreds of parsecs43,44. Note that, although the size of the most distant detectable [OIII] emission increases with AGN power, the light-weighted mean emission distance from the nucleus and the effective width of the time filtering remain mostly unknown. Moreover, [OIII] is emitted more isotropically45 than the likely highly viewing-angle dependent L_Hβ and L_5100, emitted from a potentially disk-like BLR and a geometrically thin accretion disc, respectively. Estimating SE masses from narrow emissions lines has been proposed before, and R_BLR − L relations from L_[OIII] do hold on a global scale46. The larger intrinsic scatter in the L_[OIII] from the RM-derived R_BLR − L relation (0.25 dex) compared to L_Hβ (0.17 dex) and L_5100 (0.18 dex)25 has discouraged use of L_[OIII] for SE mass estimation, but the unique dataset analysed in this work demonstrate the value of the longer time filtering provided by the narrow line region.

Our prescription for a modified virial SE mass estimator thus combines the FWHM of the broad Hβ emission line with a longer-term average of the AGN power, represented by the narrow-line luminosity L_[OIII]. Hence,

log M_BH = 2 log_10 (FWHM(Hβ) / 1000 km s^-1) + 0.49 log_10 (L_[OIII] / 10^41.69 erg s^-1) + C (2)

where β = 0.49 ± 0.04 was obtained from a RM based R_BLR − L calibration for L_[OIII]25. We calibrate the zero-point, C = 6.85 ± 0.17, from RM-based estimates of R_BLR and BH masses for 13 AGN listed in Table 2, hereafter called the RM sample. This calibration is limited by how much the RM sample represents the broader AGN population and could improve with a larger sample, but does not affect our result on the repeatability of SE masses.

Although estimating black hole masses from L_[OIII] may seem physically indirect, our results justify this approach: SE masses based on L_[OIII] show the lowest intrinsic scatter among all estimators, with a 16th-84th percentile range of 0.40 dex across two-decade separations (Fig. 5). Under the assumption that L_[OIII] remains constant across these epochs, the scatter arises solely from variations in FWHM(Hβ), with measurement errors accounting for roughly one-third of the observed spread. By contrast, SE masses based on L_Hβ or L_5100 show residuals proportional to the Hβ/[OIII] ratio, with slopes of 0.6 and 0.3 respectively. The L_[OIII]-based approach effectively removes this dependence by subtracting a unity-slope linear trend from the L_Hβ-based residuals, thereby flattening the relation and reducing uncertainties.

---

## Methods

Sample and observations
The parent sample in our study is the 6-degree Field Galaxy Survey (6dFGS39,63), which includes spectra of 125,071 galaxies at a median redshift of 0.053. These galaxies were selected from the Two Micron All Sky Survey (2MASS) Extended Source Catalogue64, complete to K < 12.65 mag, and includes miscellaneous auxiliary targets. The survey covered the Southern sky at Galactic latitude |b| ≥ 10°, with observations dating between 2001 and 2009. From the spectra of this flux-limited galaxy sample, a sample of broad emission line (BEL) AGN was identified by spectral fitting and visual inspection (6dFGS AGN40). Here, we focus on 574 objects at z < 0.1, which appear to be an near-complete sample of AGN in large galaxies at K < 12.65 mag in the Southern Sky, and use that as our historic reference sample. The objects not in our sample include AGN in dwarf galaxies below the K-band flux limit, weak AGN with BELs undetectable with 6dFGS sensitivity, or high-luminosity AGN that appear as point sources in 2MASS.

We re-observed 560 of the AGN from the 6dFGS sample with the Australian National University (ANU) 2.3 m Telescope at Siding Spring Observatory (SSO) near Coonabarabran in Australia, mostly between 2022 and 2024. These 560 objects include 137 type 1.9 Seyferts, which feature a broad Hα line without a broad Hβ line. Observations were conducted with the Wide Field Spectrograph (WiFeS65,66), an integral field spectrograph with a 38 × 25 arcsec field of view and 1 arcsec^2 spaxels. The B3000 and R3000 diffraction gratings provided coverage over 3200−9800 Å. Data reduction was performed using PyWiFeS67, a Python-based pipeline designed for WiFeS. The WiFeS spectra of the 6dFGS AGN will be separately published as a legacy resource, once observations of missing objects are complete. In addition to the 6dFGS AGN, we also observed a sample of 13 AGN with WiFeS, which have been previously reverberation-mapped to get a black hole mass estimate; references for mass estimates from the reverberation mapping studies are listed in Table 2.

The 6dFGS spectra were obtained through fibres with a 6.7 arcsec aperture, corresponding to 12.4 kpc at z = 0.1, and include narrow line emission from star formation in the host galaxy, although the [OIII] emission is usually dominated by ionisation from the AGN (> 90%)68. These spectra were observed at a spectral resolution of R~1000. We match the WiFeS observations to 6dFGS and avoid instrumental biases in the two-epoch comparison by integrating light within a 6.7 arcsec diameter region in the field of view of the WiFeS integral field unit and smoothing the spectra to the 6dFGS wavelength resolution.

Spectral decomposition
We applied the Bayesian AGN Decomposition Analysis for SDSS Spectra (BADASS369) code package to fit multiple Gaussian components to emission lines and extract broad Hβ λ4861Å and [OIII] λ5007Å luminosities from spectra, which are de-reddened for Milky Way extinction. For consistency, we fit both 6dFGS and WiFeS spectra within the same rest-frame wavelength range, 4120−5500 Å, masking 4270−4400 Å wavelength range to avoid Hγ λ4340Å emission. The spectral fitting included free parameters for an AGN power law continuum, single-stellar population host models70, and a broad and narrow optical Fe II continuum71. Broad and narrow emission lines were modelled using two Gaussian components each. The dispersion of each component was restricted to < 500 km s^-1 for the narrow Hβ and [OIII] lines, and > 500 km s^-1 for the broad Hβ component. Particularly, the second Gaussian component for the narrow emission lines aims to capture blue-shifted outflows often found in AGN69,72. The sum of the broad Hβ components was used to calculate the Hβ/[OIII] line ratio.

BADASS3 fits all spectral components simultaneously, estimating parameters and uncertainties using a Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) approach. In this work, uncertainties are derived from the posterior distributions of the MCMC chains, with the 16–50th and 50–84th percentile ranges reported as the lower and upper errors, respectively. These uncertainties are propagated when computing derived quantities such as the Hβ/[OIII] ratio and SE mass estimates.

AGN were classified as broad-lined or narrow-lined based on whether the fitting algorithm identified a broad Gaussian component for Hβ with an amplitude above the mean noise in the region. To ensure a consistent BEL comparison, we included only AGN with broad Hβ emission detectable above the noise level in both epochs. This criterion excludes type 1.9 Seyferts and the turn-off changing-look AGN identified in previous work41, which show broad Hβ emission in the 6dFGS epoch but fall below the detection threshold in the later WiFeS spectra. This final sample consists of 323 AGN. On average, the peak of the broad line is greater than the mean per-pixel noise in the Hβ fitting region by a factor of 5.6 for the WiFeS spectra, and 5.1 for the 6dFGS spectra.

Correcting for instrumental differences
Since 6dFGS was primarily a redshift survey, its spectra were not flux-calibrated, leading to spurious spectral features including those associated with the detector sensitivity, fibre interference patterns or poor sky subtraction40,63. In 28% (90/324) of the 6dFGS spectra in our sample, these features were fit with an unrealistically large broad Hβ component, mostly hitting the maximum FWHM limit of 25,000 km s^-1 allowed in the fitting algorithm, along with strong broad optical Fe II continuum, which summed up to a constant flux across the wavelength range. A similar effect, albeit much less pronounced, was observed in 7% (22/324) of the WiFeS spectra, primarily due to degeneracies in disentangling the host galaxy, optical Fe II, and AGN power-law continua. To mitigate these overestimated broad Hβ components in both datasets, we excluded such components from the combined luminosity by filtering out individual Gaussian components with FWHM > 12,000 km s^-1, a threshold well separated from the core of the FWHM distribution, which is centred at about 4500 km s^-1 and has a standard deviation of about 2000 km s^-1. The 12,000 km s^-1 limit is consistent with the FWHM(Hβ) distribution observed in a much larger AGN sample16. Particularly for the 6dFGS spectra, this broad component captures spectral artefacts, and we allow fits to reach such high line widths to effectively subtract these features.

We flux-calibrate the 6dFGS spectra such that the narrow [OIII] λ5007Å emission line flux reproduces the value from the flux-calibrated WiFeS spectra, assuming that the narrow [OIII] emission has not changed in intrinsic strength; this is a standard approach for AGN, though we acknowledge the possibility of L_[OIII] variability in a compact narrow-line region57. Any wavelength dependent offset in the continuum due to detector sensitivity is negligible due to the proximity of Hβ λ4861Å and continuum at λ5100Å to [OIII] λ5007Å.

The instruments used for the 6dFGS and WiFeS epoch observations of the AGN in our sample have never operated simultaneously, preventing a direct comparison of the spectra for identical objects. The intrinsic variability of AGN further complicates comparisons between non-simultaneous epochs. Among the spectral features, only the [OIII] λ5007Å emission line is sufficiently prominent and isolated to test for systematic differences. However, this line is also used to calibrate the 6dFGS spectra and therefore cannot serve as an independent comparison. The narrow Hβ emission, which is not expected to vary as it primarily traces star formation, shows a mean inter-epoch difference of -0.02 dex, indicating a lack of systematic offsets between the two instruments. The scatter in this difference is not directly interpretable, as the narrow line may be degenerate with the broad Hβ component.

To test whether the flat ΔFWHM(Hβ)-ΔL relation observed in our AGN sample (Fig. 3) is genuine or driven by correlated uncertainties, we simulate a control AGN sample with similar properties. We begin with 323 AGN drawn from a normal luminosity distribution with a scatter of 0.5 dex. Radii are then assigned using an R_BLR − L relation with slope 0.5 and intrinsic scatter of 0.25 dex25. For each object, we simulate a random luminosity change, ΔL, sampled from a normal distribution with scatter 0.26 dex, consistent with the observed change in the Hβ/[OIII] ratio, and compute a second-epoch R_BLR using the R_BLR − L relation. Two epochs of FWHM values are then estimated under the assumption FWHM \propto R_BLR^-0.5, i.e. a breathing relation. Measurement noise is added using the median observed scatter, rounded up to 0.05 dex for both FWHM and L.

We perform 10,000 random realisations of this distribution and compute the median slope in each case. The median slope is shown in Fig. 8 as a function of the correlation between FWHM and L measurement errors. While correlated uncertainties do increase the observed slope, even at maximum correlation the simulated slopes do not approach the observed flat distribution in Fig. 3.

NGC 5548 comparison
The legacy NGC 5548 dataset31 includes a compilation of about 1600 spectra observed from 1972 to 2015, making it the best studied Seyfert galaxy. This dataset includes fits to the Hβ, [OIII] emission lines and L_5100 continuum, which we directly use in this study. The large number of measurements with varying cadence introduces scatter in the light curves. To reduce noise, we computed the median in 30-day bins and estimated the uncertainties using the scatter per bin. The 30-day binning period is justified, as we focus solely on variability over decadal timescales, where short-term fluctuations within a month can be neglected. To compare the high-cadence dataset with our two-epoch sample, we grouped the binned NGC 5548 measurements into 2389 pairs separated by 18.5 ± 0.9 years, mirroring the separation distribution of the 6dFGS-WiFeS observations. For consistency, we adopted a constant log L_[OIII] of 41.57 (erg s^-1), derived from the flux used to normalise the spectra for the entire dataset31. The dataset has a median and 16th-84th percentile range Hβ/[OIII] ratio of 1.2 ± 0.5 over the full monitoring period. The SE mass distributions in Figure 4 uses only unbinned data between MJD 47500 and 52000, as the sparse sampling beyond this range hinders reliable spread comparisons, although the trend does not change when using the full monitoring period, with 16-84th percentile scatter of 0.245, 0.221 and 0.192 dex for L_Hβ-, L_5100- and L_[OIII]-derived masses, respectively.

Single-epoch mass estimates
We compare the reverberation-mapped black hole masses of the 13 AGN in the RM sample (Table 2) with SE mass estimates derived with L_Hβ and L_5100 as proxies for the BLR radius. The respective R_BLR − L slopes25 used for these proxies are 0.45 and 0.43, with mass estimates computed with the following equations:

log M_BH = 2 log_10 (FWHM(Hβ) / 1000 km s^-1) + 0.45 log_10 (L_Hβ / 10^42.33 erg s^-1) + 6.98 (3)

log M_BH = 2 log_10 (FWHM(Hβ) / 1000 km s^-1) + 0.43 log_10 (L_5100 / 10^44.056 erg s^-1) + 6.93 (4)

We also include a corrected relation for L_5100 using the ratio of optical Fe II and broad Hβ luminosity27:

log M_BH = 2 log_10 (FWHM(Hβ) / 1000 km s^-1) + 0.45 log_10 (L_5100 / 10^44.056 erg s^-1) + 0.35 log_10 (L_FeII / L_Hβ) + 7.05 (5)

where L_FeII is the luminosity of Fe II continuum from 4340 Å to 4680 Å as obtained from the decomposed spectral fits. The intercepts for the single-epoch mass estimators are calibrated using the RM masses of AGN in the RM sample (see Fig. 7).

SE mass estimates for the RM sample are derived from the WiFeS spectra, which were flux-calibrated using standard stars and with the full spectral resolution of R ~ 3000. However, we incorporate an additional 10% uncertainty in the luminosities to account for uncorrected variation in weather conditions. For the Hβ/[OIII] ratios shown in Fig. 7, we do not include this additional error, as the ratio remains unaffected by flux calibration uncertainties. We estimated the uncertainty of the RMS around the 1:1 line using a bootstrap approach that incorporates asymmetric uncertainties.

For SE mass estimates, the FWHM is the standard measure for the width of the full line16,46,73, whereas RM masses typically use the line dispersion, σ, of the RMS spectrum8, as it more directly traces the response-weighted BLR emission. Comparisons of the two metrics suggest that σ yields more accurate SE mass estimates, although FWHM remains broadly reliable74. We test this in our sample by examining changes in σ and in line shape, defined as S = FWHM/σ, relative to luminosity. The Hβ line dispersion is measured within a window of ± 2.5 × the median absolute deviation around the half-flux wavelength75. We find consistent trends for both FWHM and σ with respect to L_5100, but in the case of L_Hβ, the dispersion increases slightly with luminosity, corresponding to a decrease in line shape, S. This behaviour is expected, as broad emission lines tend to be better described by Lorentzian rather than Gaussian profiles at higher luminosities76. We adopt FWHM as our preferred metric, both because it remains the widely accepted measure for SE mass estimates and because our results are unchanged when using σ.

In Fig. 7, we compare the mass estimates from L_[OIII] with other estimates in the RM sample. We find that L_[OIII]-derived masses exhibit the lowest scatter among all SE estimators with 0.26 dex RMS compared to 0.30 dex for the L_Hβ-derived masses. These RMS values are calculated from the deviation from the one-to-one line after fitting for the zero-point in SE mass estimates using the RM masses. The RMS deviation is in part inflated due to uncertainties in the RM masses itself. Subtracting the measurement errors from both RM and SE masses, the intrinsic RMS deviation for the masses around the one-to-one line are 0.28, 0.29, and 0.25 dex for L_Hβ-, L_5100-, and L_[OIII]-derived masses, respectively.

### Reviewer 2

Referee Report
Title: Correcting Black Hole Masses Biased by Size Inertia in Broad Line Regions
Recommendation: Reject
Summary
This manuscript presents a study based on a two-epoch spectroscopic analysis of a sample of low-redshift AGNs, with the
goal of improving single-epoch black hole mass estimates. The approach centers on using [O III] luminosity as a proxy for
the ionizing luminosity, under the assumption that it provides a more stable indicator of the BLR radius over time.
The topic is timely and relevant, as improving the reliability of mass estimators is crucial for understanding AGN
demographics and evolution. However, there are serious concerns about both the methodology and the physical
interpretation adopted by the authors. The manuscript does not, in its current form, provide sufficient justification for its core
assumptions and does not meet the standard for publication in Nature Communications.
Major Comments
Use of FWHM and Line Width Assumptions
The most fundamental issue is the use of FWHM as a velocity width indicator in the virial mass formula, and the assumption
that black hole mass scales with the square of FWHM. This is particularly problematic in the context of a study on variability,
where FWHM responds differently than the line dispersion (sigma_line) to continuum flux changes. Since line width enters
t enters
the mass estimate as a power-law (typically squared), a poorly behaved velocity measure like FWHM introduces significant
uncertainty. The authors do not explore how FWHM compares to sigma_line under varying luminosity, nor do they justify
their choice. Simply assuming FWHM is an appropriate measure in this context is not acceptable.
Use of [O III] as a Proxy for Ionizing Flux
The use of [O III] flux as a proxy for the ionizing flux also raises concerns. While the authors mention potential advantages,
they do not consider significant drawbacks. First, [O III] luminosity reflects the time-averaged state of the continuum over
years to decades, due to both light-travel and recombination timescales. In contrast, H-beta responds on reverberation
timescales, which are much shorter and more relevant for BLR dynamics. Second, [O III] is produced by much higher energy
photons than those driving Balmer line emission. Empirically, the study by Greene et al. (2010) shows that the BLR radius
scales more tightly with H-beta luminosity than with [O III], and with less scatter. The authors have not provided any evidence
that [O III] is a better or even comparable proxy to H-beta.
Conceptual Clarifications
In the introduction, the manuscript refers to virial breathing as an “assumption,” when it is actually a predicted consequence
of the standard reverberation mapping interpretation under virial dynamics.
The statement that the variable part of the line may have a different velocity distribution than the mean line is technically
correct, but empirical studies show that line widths in mean and variable spectra are highly correlated.
--------------
Presentation of NGC 5548 and Figures
The analysis of NGC 5548 is reduced to a single data point in Figure 1, despite the long history of monitoring and variability.
It would be more informative to show a range or distribution.
Figure 2 shows changes in H-beta to [O III] ratios over a 20-year interval. The figure is difficult to interpret quantitatively as
the x-axis is not clearly defined. Moreover, a change of 0.26 dex in flux over two decades is not surprising and likely
common among AGNs.
On [O III] Variability Timescales
The claim that [O III] luminosity remains constant over human timescales is incorrect. Long-term monitoring has shown that
[O III] can vary. The more accurate assumption in prior work is that [O III] remains approximately constant over BLR
reverberation timescales, not over decades.
Terminology and References
Terminology should follow standard spectroscopic conventions. For example, the line should be referred to as [O III]
lambda5007, not lambda 5007 [O III].
Table 2 relies on outdated virial product estimates. More recent results are available in Dalla Bonta et al. (2020) for most
objects, as well as in Bentz et al. (2023, ApJ, 944, 29) for IC 4329A, Du et al. (2015, ApJ, 806, 22) for Mrk 1044, and Bentz et
al. (2021, ApJ, 906, 50) for NGC 3783.
Conclusion
The manuscript does not provide a convincing justification for its methodological choices, particularly the use of FWHM and
[O III] luminosity as primary inputs to the mass scaling relation. The results do not offer clear new insight into the physics of
AGN mass estimation and do not meet the threshold of novelty or rigor expected for this journal.

We have read “Correcting Black Hole Masses Biased by Size Inertia in Broad Line Regions” by Amrutha et al. This
manuscript reports analysis of spectral data of active galactic nuclei (AGN) that had previously been observed roughly two
decades earlier. The authors study the joint variability in the width of the H-beta line and the bolometric luminosity (as
measured by 5100 Angstrom continuum measurement and others). Based on their analysis the authors find that the joint
variability is not well described by the prevailing model (the “breathing” broad line region [BLR] model). This, in particular,
has implications for mass estimations of the AGN black holes. The authors then advocate for use of the [O III] luminosity
instead of other luminosity indicators (5100 continuum, H-beta, or combinations with Fe line complex luminosities).
We feel that the potential result is interesting, but there are a number of concerns that prevent us from being able to
determine whether the conclusions are sound. The authors will need to address our major concerns before we can
recommend publication.
*** MAJOR CONCERNS ***
A key concern is the experimental setup. The authors are comparing 6dFGS spectra taken on Schmidt with WiFeS spectra
taken on the ANU 2.3-m telescope. Small systematic differences in the different data sets (even though they were reduced
and fitted with the same procedure) could lead to the appearance of a problem in the model when it is in the data. Is it
possible to directly compare the instrumental setups for consistency? While the authors have the NGC 5548 data that should
be self-consistent, the trend within NGC 5548 is far less convincing.
Related to the above, measurement uncertainties are not addressed in the manuscript at all. It is essential to understand
how measurement uncertainties are incorporated in the analysis. This is especially important when some of the effects that
are being reported are slight (e.g., the difference between 5100 and [O III] scatter in mass measurements is only 0.035 dex).
The correlations of uncertainties between continuum and line widths is a particularly problematic aspect that needs to be
addressed. The fact that the Baldwin effect was not mentioned nor any attempt to mitigate it is particularly worrisome. It is not
possible to publish this work without a thorough examination of how this effect plays a role in the analysis.
A key test of whether what the authors see is real would be to simulate observations with realistic correlated uncertainties
that vary according to the R–L relation with an intrinsic scatter. How often does the simulated Delta FWHM vs Delta L
correlation show the same trend (or more extreme) than the data do?
Measurement uncertainties also need to be taken into account when measuring 16–18 percentiles in Fig 4 and rms in Fig 5.

The latter is better for estimating black hole masses more precisely; the former is better for understanding the physics.
